The giant floater, Pyganodon grandis, is a large freshwater mussel that begins its life as a microscopic glochidium larva. Upon eclosion from the egg capsule, the larval shell measures only approximately 0.0254 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.0254 centimeters] in total length at birth. This minuscule size is typical for unionid bivalves, which rely on a parasitic larval stage to develop before settling into the substrate. During the initial weeks following the hatching event, the glochidia must attach to the gills or fins of a suitable fish host to undergo the metamorphic transformation into a free-living juvenile. The prodissoconch stage gives way to a post-metamorphic juvenile that begins filter-feeding on phytoplankton and detritus. Growth during the first few years is relatively rapid, with juveniles reaching a total length at puberty of approximately 3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3 centimeters] based on data indicating that sexual maturation occurs around three years of age. This size threshold marks the initiation of gonadal activity and the onset of reproductive capability.

As Pyganodon grandis continues to age, its shell grows steadily towards an asymptotic size. Field surveys of lake-dwelling populations in the Great Lakes region have documented that the ultimate total length for this species reaches approximately 25.4 centimeters [Li = approximately 25.4 centimeters], a dimension that places it among the larger unionids in its habitat. This maximum shell dimension is typically attained after more than a decade of sustained somatic growth, with the rate of annual increment declining markedly in older individuals. The concomitant increase in soft tissue mass is substantial, and size-corrected estimates derived from congeneric species suggest that the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is around 317 grams [Wwi = around 317 grams]. The large adult body mass reflects the considerable investment in both shell biomineralization and the maintenance of metabolically active tissues such as the ctenidia and digestive gland. These large adults are often found burrowed in soft sediments of lakes and slow-moving rivers, where they play an important ecological role in benthic nutrient cycling by filtering suspended particles from the water column.

Reproductive output in the giant floater is tightly linked to body size and thermal regime. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], mature females at a shell length of 10.7 centimeters have been observed to produce approximately 724,000 glochidia per year [Ri = approximately 724,000 glochidia per year]. This high fecundity is a life-history strategy common to unionid mussels, offsetting the high mortality experienced during the parasitic larval phase. The reproduction rate reflects the production of a single annual brood per reproductive season [F_R_i = single annual brood per reproductive season], with females releasing their glochidia in cohesive conglutinates that attract host fish. The timing of this reproductive event is synchronized with warm summer temperatures that enhance host-fish activity and glochidial survival. The extreme fecundity per event underscores the species' reliance on a stochastic host-encounter model for successful recruitment.

Longevity in freshwater mussels is often considerable, and Pyganodon grandis is no exception. In a long-term mark-recapture study conducted at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] in a mesotrophic lake, the maximum lifespan observed for this species was estimated at approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days]. While this lifespan is shorter than that of some sympatric unionids like Elliptio complanata, which can exceed 20 years, it represents a moderate longevity consistent with its relatively rapid growth rate and early reproductive maturity. The life span constraint appears to be driven by the metabolic demands of annual reproduction and the gradual accumulation of cellular damage in the metabolically active ctenidia and mantle tissues. Natural mortality typically occurs through predation by muskrats or through senescence-related physiological decline, with older individuals exhibiting reduced filtration rates and a diminished capacity to bury themselves in the sediment. The temperature dependence of this longevity estimate highlights the influence of metabolic rate on aging in these poikilothermic bivalves.

Comparisons with other members of the family Unionidae reveal that Pyganodon grandis occupies an intermediate position along the fast-slow life-history continuum. The juvenile shell dimensions at birth of 0.0254 centimeters [Lb = 0.0254 centimeters] are broadly consistent with the glochidial size range reported for other anodontine species, reflecting a conserved parasitic life-history strategy. Similarly, the total length at puberty (3 centimeters [Lp = 3 centimeters]) aligns with the onset of reproductive maturity observed in congeneric taxa like Pyganodon cataracta, where gametogenesis commences at a comparable shell length. The ultimate total length of 25.4 centimeters [Li = 25.4 centimeters] and the associated ultimate wet weight of 317 grams [Wwi = 317 grams] place this species near the upper end of the size distribution for North American unionids, a status reflected in its common name. The daily fecundity of 724,000 glochidia per year [Ri = 724,000 glochidia per year] produced by a 10.7 cm individual at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] is within the range reported for other large-bodied mussels, while the maximum lifespan of 3650 days [am = 3650 days] at that same temperature underscores the trade-off between early reproduction and somatic persistence that defines this species' life-history strategy.
